title: NURS 1021 Unit 1 Case Study 2

question.stem: The nurse reviews the Health History and the Physical Assessment. Highlight the findings that require follow-up.
question.explanation:
Require follow-up: a swollen, warm, tense knee held in flexion, with severe pain and a 5 cm difference in circumference, is an acute hemarthrosis (bleeding into the joint), the most common bleed in severe hemophilia. Blood in the joint space raises pressure and the client holds the knee bent because that is the position of greatest joint volume. A tingling or warm feeling often comes before swelling, so pain is an early sign.

Missing two prophylactic factor VIII infusions left the client with almost no factor VIII, so a minor collision caused a major bleed. Ibuprofen inhibits platelet function and adds to the bleeding; clients with hemophilia avoid aspirin and NSAIDs. A third bleed into the same joint this year makes the right knee a target joint: repeated bleeds inflame the synovium (synovitis), which bleeds more easily and leads to hemophilic arthropathy.

Do not require follow-up: strong pedal pulses, brisk capillary refill and normal sensation show that blood flow and nerves below the knee are intact. The client is alert and oriented.

leftContent.intro: The nurse in the emergency department is caring for a 22-year-old male client with severe hemophilia A who arrived with right knee pain.

question.stem: The nurse answers the client's questions. For each statement, click to specify whether it applies to hemophilia A, hemophilia B, or both.

rows.text: Caused by a deficiency of factor IX (also called Christmas disease)
Inherited as an X-linked recessive disorder, so it occurs mainly in males
Caused by a deficiency of factor VIII and accounts for about 80% of cases
Prolonged aPTT with a normal PT and platelet count
Mild forms may be treated with desmopressin, which releases stored factor
Repeated bleeding into a joint can lead to chronic synovitis and arthropathy

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 1 1915 and the Laboratory Results.
question.explanation:
Hemophilia A is a deficiency of factor VIII and makes up about 80% of cases. Desmopressin (DDAVP) releases factor VIII and von Willebrand factor stored in endothelial cells, so it can raise the level about two- to threefold in mild hemophilia A (factor VIII 5% or higher) in clients who have been shown to respond. It cannot help when there is no factor VIII to release, as in this client's severe disease (less than 1%), or in hemophilia B.

Hemophilia B (Christmas disease) is a deficiency of factor IX.

Both are X-linked recessive, so males are mainly affected and the daughters of an affected male are carriers. Factors VIII and IX both belong to the intrinsic pathway, so both prolong the aPTT while the PT (extrinsic pathway) and platelet count stay normal; only factor assays tell them apart. Both cause the same bleeding: hemarthroses, muscle hematomas and, after even minor head trauma, intracranial hemorrhage. Severity depends on the factor level: below 1% severe (spontaneous bleeding), 1% to 5% moderate (bleeding after minor trauma), 5% to 49% mild (bleeding after surgery or dental extraction).

leftContent.intro: The nurse in the emergency department is caring for a 22-year-old male client with severe hemophilia A who arrived with right knee pain.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: A prolonged aPTT with a normal PT, INR and platelet count points to a defect in the [[drop0]]. Because the aPTT corrects when the client's plasma is mixed with normal plasma, the cause is [[drop1]]. The nurse's priority is [[drop2]].

options.text: formation of the platelet plug
extrinsic pathway of coagulation
breakdown of clots by fibrinolysis
intrinsic pathway of coagulation
an antibody that inhibits factor VIII
consumption of clotting factors
a missing clotting factor
a lack of vitamin K
teaching about the inheritance of hemophilia
stopping the bleeding into the knee
restoring knee range of motion
preventing infection in the knee

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 1 1940 and the Vital Signs.
question.explanation:
Reading the tests: the aPTT measures the intrinsic and common pathways (factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, then X, V, II and fibrinogen); the PT and INR measure the extrinsic and common pathways (factor VII, then X, V, II, fibrinogen). A normal platelet count and fibrinogen with a prolonged aPTT and normal PT localize the problem to the intrinsic factors, which include VIII and IX.

Mixing study: normal plasma supplies the missing factor, so a factor deficiency corrects. An inhibitor (an antibody against factor VIII, which develops in about 30% of clients with severe hemophilia A treated with factor) would also block the factor in the normal plasma, so the aPTT would stay prolonged. Vitamin K deficiency and consumption of factors (as in DIC) prolong the PT as well.

Priority: the knee is still bleeding (circumference 42 to 43 cm, pain 8/10, rising heart rate). Ongoing bleeding threatens the joint now and increases blood loss; it is stopped by replacing factor VIII. Range of motion, infection risk and genetics teaching come after the bleeding is controlled.

question.stem: Which interventions should the nurse include in the client's plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give hydromorphone IV or acetaminophen PO for pain as prescribed
Measure the knee circumference and check pulses and sensation in the foot regularly
Start active range-of-motion exercises of the knee tonight to prevent stiffness
Apply a warm compress to the knee to relax the surrounding muscles
Give the factor VIII infusion as soon as possible
Give ibuprofen PO, since it eases both pain and joint inflammation
Apply the wrapped ice pack to the knee for 15 to 20 minutes at a time
Keep the right knee at rest in the splint and elevated

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 1 2000 and the Orders.
question.explanation:
Include: factor VIII replacement is the treatment that stops the bleeding, and it is given as early as possible; a dose of 50 units/kg raises factor VIII to about 100%, since each unit/kg raises it about 2% (Option 5). Rest, splinting and elevation limit further bleeding and pain (Option 8). Cold causes local vasoconstriction and eases pain (Option 7). Acetaminophen and opioids relieve pain without affecting platelets; hydromorphone is given IV, never IM (Option 1). Circumference, pain and neurovascular checks show whether the bleeding is controlled and detect compression of nerves or vessels (Option 2).

Do not include: NSAIDs and aspirin inhibit platelet function and increase bleeding (Option 6). Active exercise while the joint is still bleeding causes more bleeding; physiotherapy starts once pain and swelling settle (Option 3). Heat dilates blood vessels and increases bleeding (Option 4).

leftContent.intro: The nurse in the emergency department is caring for a 22-year-old male client with severe hemophilia A who arrived with right knee pain.

question.stem: Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Give acetaminophen for the headache and recheck the neurologic status in 1 hour
Transport the client to CT first, since factor VIII is needed only if a bleed is confirmed
Anticipate a prescription for a factor VIII dose to be given immediately, before the CT scan
Apply an ice pack to the left temple and keep the client on bed rest

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 2 0610 and the Vital Signs.
question.explanation:
Correct (Option 3): in a person with hemophilia, “even a trivial blow to the head” can cause intracranial hemorrhage, and a headache after head trauma is treated as a possible bleed. Factor replacement to about 100% begins immediately, before the CT scan or any other test is completed; waiting for imaging lets a bleed expand. The client's factor VIII level is falling since last night's dose, so a new dose is needed now.

Incorrect: delaying factor until the CT confirms a bleed risks a fatal hemorrhage (Option 2). Treating the headache and waiting an hour misses the window to treat; a normal Glasgow Coma Scale now does not rule out a slowly expanding bleed (Option 1). Ice and rest do nothing to stop an intracranial bleed (Option 4). The nurse continues frequent neurologic checks once factor is given.

question.stem: For each finding, click to specify whether the client's condition has improved or not improved compared with admission.
question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 2 0800 and Day 4 1000, the Vital Signs, and the Laboratory Results.
question.explanation:
Improved: knee circumference fell from 42 to 38 cm (right) as blood in the joint is reabsorbed; pain fell from 8/10 to 2/10; the knee now lacks only 10° of extension instead of 30°. Factor VIII replacement corrected the aPTT (68 s to 31 s) and the trough factor VIII is 62%, within the 50% to 80% target for a severe joint bleed.

Not improved: hemoglobin fell from 138 to 121 g/L, reflecting the blood lost into the knee. It is now stable, but it is lower than on admission and is rechecked; a further fall would suggest another bleed.

Before discharge: the nurse reinforces regular prophylaxis (missed doses caused this bleed), treating any bleed early with home factor, avoiding aspirin and NSAIDs, wearing medical identification, regular dental care, and seeking care at once for headache, vomiting or drowsiness after any head injury.

description: 22-year-old male with severe hemophilia A and an acute knee hemarthrosis after missed prophylaxis, then a minor head injury: coagulation tests (PT/INR, aPTT, mixing study, factor assays), hemophilia A versus B, factor replacement.

authorReview.note: New case written by Claude on 24 Nov 2026 (NURS 1021 Unit 1, batch 1); checked against Merck Manual Professional (Hemophilia, Jul 2025). Please review: fibrinogen (2.0–4.0 g/L) and factor VIII/IX activity (50%–150%) reference ranges (not in the MCC list); factor VIII doses (50 units/kg, then 25 units/kg every 12 hours); ice for hemarthrosis (standard nursing teaching; some guidelines are less firm).
